correctness.rationale: For \(\theta=\pi/(4n)\), the regular polygon lies between Euclidean disks of radii \(\cos\theta\) and \(1\), giving identity distortion at most \(\sec\theta\). The published Banach–Mazur inequality therefore gives \(C_{\mathrm{NJ}}[X_{4n}]\le\sec^2\theta\). A symmetric adjacent vertex pair has sum norm \(2\) and difference norm \(2\tan\theta\); at \(t=1\) this gives the matching lower bound. The vertical difference is a facet-normal direction exactly because \(4n\) is divisible by four. These steps prove the full quantifier \(n\ge1\); the finite checker is not used as an infinite certificate.

The closest exact polygon papers found treat only the regular octagon and different or more parameterized constants. Targeted semantic and web searches did not return a theorem covering the full regular \(4n\)-gonal skew constant. The octagon case is treated as prior coverage; the claimed contribution is the all-\(n\) family and endpoint-saturation statement.

value.rationale: This is an exact natural invariant on the complete infinite family of regular \(4n\)-gonal normed planes, not an arbitrary parameter slice. It identifies a structural saturation mechanism: the sharp Banach–Mazur distortion bound is attained by the skew constant and the optimizing skew parameter collapses to \(t=1\). The formula also quantifies the Euclidean limit through \(\sec^2(\pi/(4n))\to1\). The result extends beyond isolated octagon computations while remaining self-contained and directly reusable as a benchmark for skew geometric constants.
